title: Test out of Part C
crib:
These are the R behaviours the questions rely on.

- **A list** holds named pieces of any size and type. `x$name` takes one
  piece out, using the name exactly as written. A name that isn't there
  quietly gives `NULL` — nothing — with no error. `x[["name"]]` does the
  same, and inside the double brackets a variable holding a name is looked
  up.
- **`t.test(x, y)`** compares two groups and returns a list. Its printout
  labels the groups `x` and `y`, by the order you gave them, not by your
  names. It leaves missing values out without saying so.
- **Scientific notation**: `5e-04` means 5 × 10⁻⁴.
- **`for (v in values) { ... }`** runs the code in the braces once for each
  value. Inside a loop, results aren't shown unless something prints them.
- **`if (condition) { ... }`** needs exactly one TRUE or FALSE. Giving it
  several values, or `NA`, is an error.
- **Packages** add functions. Install one once per computer, with
  `install.packages("name")`; load it in every new session, with
  `library(name)`.
- **dplyr**: `filter(df, condition)` keeps rows where the condition is TRUE
  and drops rows where it's `NA`. Inside its functions, column names are
  written on their own. `mutate()` and `filter()` return a new data frame
  and never change the one you gave them. `select()` keeps the columns you
  name.
- **`|>`**, the pipe, hands what's on its left to the function on its
  right, as the first argument. Read it as *and then*.
context:
Questions 1–4 use this t-test result, stored as `result`:

```
drug    <- c(128, 134, 121, 139, 125, 131, 127, 136)
placebo <- c(142, 138, 149, 135, 144, 151, 140, 146)
result  <- t.test(drug, placebo)
```

```
        Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  drug and placebo
t = -4.5272, df = 13.874, p-value = 0.0004844
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -19.164014  -6.835986
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
  130.125   143.125 
```

Questions 9–12 use this data frame, `patients`:

```
  age sbp discharged
1  67 142       TRUE
2  54 118      FALSE
3  71  NA      FALSE
4  48 131       TRUE
5  62 156       TRUE
```

items.title: Taking out the p-value
items.prompt: Which line gives just the p-value from `result`?

options.feedback:
Right. `result` is a list, and `$` takes out one piece by its exact
name: `p.value`.

A shortened name is risky. Here `p` could mean `p.value` or
`parameter`, so R gives `NULL` — nothing — without an error. Write
the full name.

The printout says "p-value", but the piece inside the list is named
`p.value`, with a full stop. A name that isn't there gives `NULL`.

That takes the first piece of the list, which is the t statistic, not
the p-value. Use the piece's name.

items.title: Which group is which
items.prompt:
The printout ends with `mean of x` 130.125 and `mean of y` 143.125. Which
group had the mean of 130.125?

options.feedback:
Right. `x` and `y` are `t.test()`'s first two arguments, and `drug`
was written first. The printout uses those labels, not your names, so
only the order of the call tells you which is which.
`drug` was written first, so it's `x`. `mean of x` is the drug group.

Not from the printout alone — but you can from the call. `x` is the
first argument, and `drug` came first.

Right. `5e-04` is 5 × 10⁻⁴. R switches to this notation for very small
numbers. Rounded to three places instead, it would print `0` — and a
p-value is never really zero, so report it as *p* < 0.001.

The `e-04` means × 10⁻⁴, so the 5 moves four places to the right of
the decimal point: 0.0005.

That would be `5e+04`. The minus sign makes it small: 5 × 10⁻⁴, which
is 0.0005.
It's a number, written compactly: 5 × 10⁻⁴, or 0.0005.

items.title: A missing value in a t-test
items.prompt:
One placebo reading is changed to `NA`. `mean(placebo)` now gives `NA`.
What does `t.test(drug, placebo)` do?

options.text: Leaves the missing reading out and runs on the rest, without saying so
options.feedback:
Right. `mean()` refuses to guess; `t.test()` drops the missing value
and carries on. The only clue is that the placebo mean and the
degrees of freedom change.

A reasonable guess, but `t.test()` behaves differently: it drops the
missing reading and runs on what's left, without a word.
No error. It drops the missing reading and runs on the other seven.

items.title: A loop without print()

options.feedback:
Right. Inside a loop, results aren't shown unless something prints
them. Each subtraction happens, and each answer is thrown away.

That's what you'd see with `print(r - 10)`. Without it, a loop shows
nothing.
Not even the last. Nothing inside a loop is shown unless it's printed.

That's what `c(118, 142) - 10` would print, outside a loop. Inside
one, nothing is shown unless it's printed.

items.title: An if given two values
items.prompt:
```r
x <- c(118, 142)
if (x > 140) print("high")
```

What happens?

options.text: An error — the condition has more than one value
options.feedback:
Right. `x > 140` gives two answers, and `if` needs exactly one. For an
answer per value, use `ifelse()`.

That's the intention, but `if` isn't a loop. It takes one TRUE or
FALSE, and two is an error.

options.text: It checks only the first value, and prints nothing
options.feedback:
Older versions of R did that, with a warning. Since R 4.2 it's an
error.

items.title: An if meets a missing value

options.text: It stops with an error at the missing value, and never checks 156
options.feedback:
Right. `NA > 140` is `NA`, and `if` needs a definite TRUE or FALSE.
The loop stops on the second value, so 156 — which really is high —
is never looked at.

`if` can't skip a missing value. The loop stops at it, before
reaching 156.

There is an error, at the missing value: *missing value where
TRUE/FALSE needed*.

items.title: A name held in a variable
items.prompt:
```r
name <- "p.value"
```

Which line gives the p-value?

options.feedback:
Right. Double brackets work out what's inside them first, so
`result[[name]]` becomes `result[["p.value"]]`.

`$` never looks inside a variable. It takes `name` as the piece's
actual name, finds no piece called that, and gives `NULL`.

options.text: Either — they do the same thing
options.feedback:
They would if the name were typed out. With the name held in a
variable, only `[[ ]]` looks it up; `$name` gives `NULL`.

items.title: A new session
items.prompt:
Yesterday you installed and loaded dplyr. Today, in a new R session,
`mutate()` gives `could not find function "mutate"`. What's missing?

options.feedback:
Right. Installing lasts; loading lasts only until R closes. Every new
session needs `library()` again.

It's still installed. What resets with each session is whether it's
loaded.

It's spelled correctly. The function exists, but its package isn't
loaded in this session.

items.title: dplyr's filter and a missing value
items.prompt:
Patient 3's systolic is missing. How many rows does this give?

```r
filter(patients, sbp > 140)
```

options.feedback:
Right. `filter()` keeps rows where the condition is TRUE and drops the
rest, including the one where it's `NA`. Square brackets,
`patients[patients$sbp > 140, ]`, would give three — adding a row of
`NA`s. Same question, two tools, two answers.

That's what square brackets give, with an extra row of `NA`s.
`filter()` drops the missing row instead.

options.text: An error — the column has a missing value
options.feedback: No error. `filter()` drops the row with the missing value, silently.

items.title: A column that wasn't kept
items.prompt:
You run `mutate(patients, map = sbp / 2)`. Afterwards, does `patients`
have a `map` column?

options.text: No — mutate() returns a new data frame, and nothing stored it
options.feedback:
Right. dplyr's functions never change the data frame you give them.
To keep the result: `patients <- mutate(patients, ...)`.

It hands back a new data frame instead. Unless that's stored, it's
printed and gone.
It isn't there at all. Nothing stored the new data frame.

items.title: Reading a pipeline
items.prompt:
What comes out?

```r
patients |>
  filter(discharged) |>
  select(age)
```

options.text: A one-column data frame of ages: 67, 48 and 62
options.feedback:
Right. Take `patients`, *and then* keep the discharged rows, *and
then* keep only the `age` column.

options.text: The ages of all five patients
options.feedback:
The `filter(discharged)` step runs first, keeping only the three who
went home.

options.text: The three discharged patients, with every column
options.feedback: The last step, `select(age)`, keeps only the `age` column.

Those are the patients still in hospital. `filter(discharged)` keeps
the ones where `discharged` is TRUE.
